---
order: 4
unit: ai
title: Train a recycling sorter
summary: Train a picture model in the Pattern Trainer, then test it on photos it has never seen. It works on photos like its training photos and fails on others, so to fix a model you change its data.
language: makecode
hook: "Recycling centres use cameras and trained models to sort paper from plastic on a fast conveyor belt. Before a centre trusts one, someone has to test it on items it has never seen."
---
A recycling centre wants a camera that sorts **Paper** from **Plastic**. You will train a model in the **Pattern Trainer**, then test it on the board's photos: paper and plastic items your model has never seen, in different places and light.

**To train a model:** open the [Pattern Trainer](https://tools.learningwaypoints.com/trainer/) in a new tab and choose **Pictures**. Name the first class **Paper**, then **+ Add a class** and name it **Plastic**. Add about 20 photos of each (hold the item up to the camera and **Hold to record**, or **Upload photos**), and click **Train model**. Then click **Download my_model.json**, and on the board click **Open your model file** and choose it.

**No webcam, or no paper and plastic on your desk?** Download photos to upload instead (unzip them, then in each class choose **Upload photos** and select every photo in its folder): [plain photos](../../../_playground-board/media/classifier/recycling/recycling-biased.zip) and [varied photos](../../../_playground-board/media/classifier/recycling/recycling-good.zip).

## Predict

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Students expect a model that works on their own desk to have learned what paper is. Committing to that first makes the messy-bench result mean something."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Your model gets your own items right almost every time on the webcam. The board tests it on other paper and plastic photographed on a messy bench. Its score on the messy bench will be…"
  options: ["Much lower than on plain backgrounds", "About the same: it has learned what paper is", "Exactly 50%: it guesses", "Higher: more objects help it"]
  actual: "Much lower. The model learned from photos on one plain background, so the background is part of what it learned. On a messy bench it is often wrong."
```

## Train and test

```step
stage: run
insight: "Seeing the plain and messy scores side by side settles the prediction: the model works on photos like its training photos."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#try", height: 760 }
check: { type: board, text: "Train two classes (Paper and Plastic) on one plain background, open your model file and test it.", when: "n_total = 16" }
```

Train **Paper** and **Plastic** with about 20 photos each, all on the same plain desk (or upload the **plain photos**). Download your model and **Open your model file** on the board. Compare the **plain background** and **messy bench** scores.

## Read the results

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "Accuracy by group shows where a model fails, not just how much; what the failures share points to what was missing from the training data."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "A model gets 23 of 32 test photos right. What is its accuracy, as a percentage (to the nearest whole number)?"
      answer: 72
      tolerance: 0.5
      explain: "Accuracy is correct ÷ total: 23 ÷ 32 = 0.72, or 72%."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "This model scores: plain 8/8, messy 4/8, low light 5/8, not paper or plastic 0/8. Its training photos were all on one plain desk. Why does it fail on the messy bench?"
      options: ["It cannot tell the item from the background it was trained on", "It needs more training epochs", "Messy photos are harder for every model, so nothing can be done", "It has forgotten what paper is"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Changing settings does not show it new backgrounds. What was missing from its photos?", "A model trained on messy backgrounds does much better on them.", "It never knew what paper is: it only knows the photos it was given."]
      explain: "Every training photo had the same plain desk, so the desk is part of what the model learned. On a cluttered bench it is guessing."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Another model scores well everywhere except low light. Which fix is most likely to work?"
      options: ["Add training photos taken in low light", "Add more photos on the same bright desk", "Train for longer", "Rename the classes"]
      answer: 0
      explain: "Look for what the failures share (low light), then add training photos that have it. Change the data, not the settings."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Sam's model scores 50% on the messy bench. Sam adds 100 more photos of the same items on the same desk. The messy score doesn't change. What went wrong?"
      options: ["The new photos were like the old ones, so they added no variety", "100 photos is too many", "Sam needed to delete the old photos first", "The board's test is unfair"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "More photos can help, but only if they are different from the ones the model already has.", "The old photos are fine; they just don't show any other backgrounds.", "Every model is tested on the same photos."]
      explain: "More of the same data teaches the model nothing new. Sam needs photos on different backgrounds."
```

### Accuracy

**Accuracy** is the number correct divided by the number tested. A score for each **group** of test photos (plain, messy, low light) shows **where** a model fails, not just how often.

### What the failures share

To find what is wrong, look at the ✗ photos and ask what they have in common that is not the item: the background, the light, the angle. Then compare that with the training photos.

| Step | What to write | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | overall = 23 ÷ 32 = 72% | Accuracy is correct ÷ total |
| 2 | plain 8/8, messy 4/8, low light 5/8, neither 0/8 | Groups show where it fails |
| 3 | The messy failures all have a cluttered background | Look for what the failures share |
| 4 | The training photos were all on one plain desk | The model can't tell item from background |
| 5 | Fix: add training photos on cluttered backgrounds | Change the data, not the settings |

### Your turn

Same model, different results: it fails only in low light. Work through steps 3 to 5 for it.

### Sam's model

## Fix the data

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Each change to the training data, one at a time, shows its own effect on the scores."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#all", height: 760 }
tasks:
  - check: { type: board, text: "Retrain with photos on at least three different backgrounds. Get the messy bench to 75% or more.", when: "acc_messy >= 0.75" }
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "You train Paper with 60 photos and Plastic with 10. Which way does the model lean when it is unsure?"
      options: ["Towards Paper", "Towards Plastic", "Neither: the number of photos doesn't matter"]
      answer: 0
      explain: "A class with many more examples wins most close calls. Give each class about the same number of photos."
  - check: { type: board, text: "The model labels a can or a bottle of glass as paper or plastic. Add a Neither class and get the 'not paper or plastic' group to 75% or more.", when: "has_neither = 1 and acc_neither >= 0.75" }
```

### Backgrounds

Retrain your model with photos of the items on **at least three different backgrounds** (or upload the **varied photos**). Download it again and open the new file on the board.

### Unbalanced classes

### Neither

Look at the **not paper or plastic** group: the model gives a can or a jar a label anyway, often with high confidence. A model always picks one of its classes. Add a third class called **Neither** with photos of other things (cans, glass, fruit), retrain and test again.

## Diagnose

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Naming the problem and the data fix without training again checks that the idea transfers."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A model was trained on photos taken at midday by a window. It scores 100% plain, 88% messy, 25% low light. What is the problem, and the fix?"
      options: ["No dim photos in training: add photos taken in low light", "Too few classes: add a Neither class", "Too many photos: delete some", "The test is unfair: ignore low light"]
      answer: 0
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A model scores 90% on paper and plastic but labels every can as Plastic with 95% confidence. What is the problem, and the fix?"
      options: ["It has no class for other things: add a Neither class", "High confidence means it is right: nothing to fix", "It needs more plastic photos", "Cans are too shiny for any model"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "Find a ✗ with a long confidence bar: a model can be confident and wrong.", "More plastic photos would make it even more likely to say Plastic.", "A model trained with cans in a Neither class learns them."]
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Paper has 80 photos and Plastic has 15. The model calls most plastic items Paper. What is the problem, and the fix?"
      options: ["The classes are unbalanced: give each class about the same number of photos", "Plastic is harder to see: add a filter", "It needs a Neither class", "Retrain with the same photos"]
      answer: 0
```

## Make a sorter you would trust

```step
stage: make
insight: "Meeting a target on every group, not just overall, is what testing before trusting means."
try: { playground: board, starter: "boards.yml#all", height: 760 }
check: { type: board, text: "Build a sorter that gets 80% or more overall and 75% or more in low light.", when: "acc_all >= 0.8 and acc_dim >= 0.75" }
```

Use what you found: varied backgrounds and light, balanced classes, and a **Neither** class. Then ask a classmate to bring three items your model has never seen. Does it still work?

## Evaluate

```step
stage: info
check: { type: reflect, text: "I wrote which items or conditions my sorter would still get wrong, and what a recycling centre should test before trusting it." }
```

Write one or two sentences: which items or conditions your sorter would still get wrong, and what a real recycling centre would need to test before trusting it.

**Revision summary**

- A model learns only from the examples you give it: it works on inputs like its training data and fails on others.
- **Accuracy** = correct ÷ total. Test on photos the model has never seen, and look at each **group**, not just the overall score.
- Find what the failures share, then **change the data**: more variety, balanced classes, a class for "none of these".
- A model always picks one of its classes, and it can be confident and wrong.

```teacher
summary: Students train a Paper/Plastic picture model in the Pattern Trainer,
  test it on photos it has never seen, and fix it by changing the training data.
time: 50
timing: Predict 3 min · Train and test 12 min · Read the results 10 min · Fix
  the data 15 min · Diagnose 4 min · Make and Evaluate 6 min
goals:
  - I can train an image model and test it on photos it has never seen.
  - I can work out accuracy, overall and for each group of test photos.
  - I can find what a model's mistakes share and fix it by changing its training
    data.
before: >
  **The idea:** a model learns only from the examples it is given. It works on
  new inputs that look like its training photos and fails on ones that don't.
  The fix is always in the data, not the settings.


  **How it works:** students train in the **Pattern Trainer**
  (tools.learningwaypoints.com/trainer/, free, no account), click **Download
  my_model.json**, and open that file on the board with **Open your model
  file**. The board keeps it in the browser, so the next lessons start with it.
  The board tests the model on 40 fixed photos it has never seen, in five
  groups: plain background, messy bench, low light, crumpled or at odd angles,
  and things that are neither paper nor plastic. Checks tick on the board's
  scores, not on the training.


  **Before class:** on a student laptop on the school network, open the Pattern
  Trainer, train a tiny model, download it and open it on the board. The trainer
  and the board each load about 35 MB from tools.learningwaypoints.com the first
  time, so check the network allows it. Bring a box of clean paper and plastic
  (and a few cans, jars or fruit) so every desk has variety.


  **Privacy:** training happens in the browser and photos never leave the
  computer (the trainer's Privacy page shows how to check). `my_model.json`
  holds class names and numbers, no photos, and stays on the student's computer.
  Train on objects, not faces.


  **Teachable Machine still works:** a student who trains there can export with
  **Upload my model** and paste the link into the box under **Open your model
  file**. Its webcam is mirrored; the Pattern Trainer's is not.


  **No webcam?** The lesson links two folders of photos to upload instead:
  **plain** (30 per class on a white board: trains the biased model) and
  **varied** (messy benches, low light, odd angles and a Neither class: trains a
  good one). The photos come from TrashNet (MIT licence); the messy benches and
  low light are made from them.


  The test photos are similar in style to the downloadable ones, so a model
  trained only on the varied folder can do well without the webcam. That is
  fine: the point is what changes the scores.
running:
  - "Predict: take a show of hands. Most expect 'about the same'."
  - "Train and test: give students 8 minutes to train. Plain is usually high and
    messy low. Ask: what is different about the messy photos?"
  - "Read the results: model the table live with one student's results, one line
    at a time. Then students do the low-light version themselves."
  - "Fix the data: one change at a time. Students who add more photos of the
    same desk see no change: that is Sam's mistake, so point back to it."
  - "Neither: ask what label a can gets, and how confident the model is."
  - "Evaluate: collect a few answers about what a recycling centre should test."
stuck:
  - see: The board says the file is not a model file, or is a project file.
    ask: Did you click Download my_model.json (not Save project)?
    fix: Download the model and open my_model.json on the board.
  - see: The board says the picture model didn't load.
    ask: Can this computer open tools.learningwaypoints.com?
    fix: Ask for the site to be allowed on the school network, then reload.
  - see: The board says the model has no class called Paper or Plastic.
    ask: What did you name your classes in the Pattern Trainer?
    fix: Rename the classes to Paper and Plastic, train again, download and open the
      new file.
  - see: A student keeps adding photos but the messy score doesn't change.
    ask: Are the new photos different from the old ones?
    fix: "Take photos on new backgrounds: a book, a jumper, a cluttered pencil
      case."
  - see: A student wants to change the training settings (epochs, learning rate) to
      fix it.
    ask: Did the model see any messy backgrounds?
    fix: Change the photos, not the settings.
stretch: Add a fourth class (Cardboard or Glass). Which pairs of classes does
  the model mix up most, and why?
support: "Use the downloaded photos instead of the webcam: plain first (the
  biased model), then varied."
leads: >
  Next: send the model's labels to a micro:bit that sorts with a servo flap.


  Real world: automated recycling sorters, and any camera system tested on
  people or places it wasn't trained on (who might it fail for?).
exit:
  q: A model scores 95% on its own desk and 50% in the canteen. What do you do?
  a: Find what the canteen photos have that the training photos don't (background,
    light), and add training photos like that.
explain: >
  A **model learns only from the examples you give it**. It works on new photos
  that look like its training photos and fails on ones that don't.


  - **Accuracy** = correct ÷ total, on photos the model has never seen.

  - Look at each **group** to see where it fails, and what the failures share.

  - To fix it, **change the data**: more variety, balanced classes, a class for
  "none of these".
struggle: Accepting that a model trained on one desk fails on a messy bench. Ask
  what the test photos have that the training photos don't, before adding more
  data.
```
